first_impression.reaction: My assistant shortlisted this because the family office has already raised an agreement, and with family in Dubai, Sydney and London nobody is sure which country's rules apply. The first screen is sober and correct, and it says straight away that this is not legal advice. Good. Our lawyers will do the real work, so I'm not reading this to learn the law. I'm reading it to see whether a wedding company can handle a delicate subject without being clumsy. Her summary for me: in Australia it's a binding financial agreement, each of us needs our own Australian lawyer, an agreement signed overseas is not automatically recognised there, and start early. I read the intro, the cross-country parts and the close myself. She skimmed the requirements.

journey.quote: This is general information, not legal advice, and each partner needs their own independent legal advice.
journey.reaction: Correct and calm. A planner pretending to know family law would lose me immediately. This one doesn't.

journey.section: Why some prenups are set aside
journey.quote: [Victoria Legal Aid](https://www.legalaid.vic.gov.au/agreement-about-dividing-property) says financial agreements are legally binding unless it can be proved that: there was fraud; the agreement is not practical; it did not follow the formal requirements under the Family Law Act; there has been a major and unexpected change affecting a child; one person acted in an unfair way; one person did not follow the agreement; or property covered was taken by the government because of criminal activity.
journey.reaction: That's the second list of the same grounds in a row. My assistant stopped here. Criminal confiscation is not something I want to read about on a wedding site.

journey.section: One partner has property or super to protect
journey.quote: [Moneysmart](https://moneysmart.gov.au/family-and-relationships/relationships-and-money) says that if you have assets to protect, such as property or super, you can ask your partner to sign a binding financial agreement.
journey.reaction: 'Property or super' is the language of a couple with a flat and a retirement fund. It's not wrong, but it tells me who the page imagines is reading it.

journey.quote: Legal Aid NSW says an agreement can protect an inheritance a partner may receive in future.
journey.reaction: This is the actual reason families like mine have these conversations. Brief, and not awkward about it.

journey.section: Couples living or marrying across countries
journey.quote: For couples with a home, a business or family on two continents, that single point is often what starts the conversation with a lawyer.
journey.reaction: Three continents in our case, but yes. This is the first line that feels written with us in mind.

journey.section: How to get a prenup and when to sign before the wedding
journey.quote: The work happens between you and two separate lawyers, and the wedding calendar is the thing to plan around: talk to your lawyer early, well before the final weeks fill with fittings, flights and seating plans.
journey.reaction: Practical. Timing is the bit our office will care about, because the wedding timeline belongs to the planner and the agreement belongs to the lawyers.

journey.section: Prenups for destination weddings and international couples
journey.quote: Legal Aid NSW says a financial agreement made overseas won't be automatically recognised in Australia, even if the agreement says otherwise.
journey.reaction: This is what my assistant flagged for the family office. One line, clear, worth the click.

journey.section: Prenups for destination weddings and international couples
journey.quote: The agreement stays with your lawyers.
journey.reaction: Exactly right. I don't want a planner anywhere near this document. Saying so plainly is the most discreet line on the page.

journey.section: Prenups for destination weddings and international couples
journey.quote: The celebration is different work: one Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel and vendors with you as a single point of contact, anywhere in the world, through [Wedded Concierge](https://weddedwonderland.com/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=prenup&utm_content=secondary).
journey.reaction: 'Anywhere in the world' suits us. 'One Wedded Advisor' for 300 guests from three countries, with our own security? Nothing here tells me they've done anything like our scale, or how they keep things private.

journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel and vendors with you, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: Again the reassurance about fees. That isn't my worry. I want to know what's possible.

journey.quote: For ideas while the paperwork settles, browse [Wedded Wonderland magazines and planning guides](https://weddedwonderland.com/magazine?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=prenup&utm_content=magnet).
journey.reaction: Calling a prenup 'the paperwork' and then sending me to browse magazines is a bit light for the subject. It's a standard sign-off.

unanswered_questions: Have they planned a celebration abroad for 200 to 400 guests, with exclusive use and our own security working with the venue's?
Does one Wedded Advisor work alone, or is there a team behind them at our scale?
How do they handle confidentiality? A planner learns a lot about a family's affairs during a wedding like ours, even if they never see the agreement.
Is there a private or referral route to someone senior, rather than the Wedded Concierge web page?
Can the wedding timeline be coordinated with our lawyers' timing without the planner needing details of the agreement?

turn_offs_found.quote: [Victoria Legal Aid](https://www.legalaid.vic.gov.au/agreement-about-dividing-property) says financial agreements are legally binding unless it can be proved that: there was fraud; the agreement is not practical; it did not follow the formal requirements under the Family Law Act; there has been a major and unexpected change affecting a child; one person acted in an unfair way; one person did not follow the agreement; or property covered was taken by the government because of criminal activity.
turn_offs_found.why: Over-explaining. It repeats the Legal Aid NSW list straight before it, and a wedding brand reciting grounds like criminal confiscation reads as eager to show its homework, not as calm expertise. Our lawyers will cover this.

turn_offs_found.quote: [Moneysmart](https://moneysmart.gov.au/family-and-relationships/relationships-and-money) says that if you have assets to protect, such as property or super, you can ask your partner to sign a binding financial agreement.
turn_offs_found.why: Leading the 'who it suits' section with property and super, from a government money-guidance service, frames the page for a standard client. Inheritance and family on several continents are further down, and that's where people like me are.

turn_offs_found.quote: Your Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel and vendors with you, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins.
turn_offs_found.why: Putting the fee in the closing pitch reads as value reassurance for a budget-conscious couple. It makes the brand sound like a package, not a team that can deliver something at our level.

would_share_with: Our family office, for the point that an agreement made overseas is not automatically recognised in Australia, and the advice to start early
My fiance's side in London, so both families' lawyers are working from the same starting point

cta_reaction.why: They handle a delicate subject with restraint and keep out of the legal side, which I respect. But nothing speaks to scale, security or privacy, and the close is pitched at someone worried about fees. I wouldn't fill in a web form. With a referral from someone we trust, my assistant would make the call.

top_3_changes: In 'Why some prenups are set aside', keep one list of grounds and cut the second (the Victoria Legal Aid sentence), or reduce it to a single line saying Victoria Legal Aid gives a similar list, with the link. It removes the most over-explained part of the page.

In 'Who needs a prenup? Couples it often suits', move 'Expected inheritances' and 'Couples living or marrying across countries' above 'One partner has property or super to protect', so the section opens with family wealth and families across countries, not a standard property-and-super case.

In 'Planning the celebration', lead with 'anywhere in the world', move 'with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins' out of the lead sentence, and add one line inviting couples with large guest lists, families in several countries or privacy needs to say so when they first get in touch. Consider replacing 'while the paperwork settles' with wording that doesn't make the agreement sound minor.
